content: The glottal stop, also known as the voiceless glottal plosive, is a specific type of consonantal sound that is utilized in numerous spoken languages. This sound is represented in the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) by a designated symbol. The glottal stop is produced when the vocal cords are pressed together to momentarily block the flow of air, which is then released. A common example of this sound can be observed in the break between the syllables of the interjection uh-oh. Although the glottal stop is not considered a phoneme in English, it is present in nearly all English dialects as an allophone of the /t/ sound. For instance, in some dialects, the /t/ in bottle may be pronounced as a glottal stop. Interestingly, while English speakers produce this sound effortlessly and frequently in daily speech, it often requires detailed explanation when teaching it to English speakers in the context of other languages, such as Arabic. In traditional Romanization systems for many languages, including Arabic, the glottal stop is transcribed using an apostrophe. This practice is the origin of the IPA symbol for the glottal stop. In contrast, many Polynesian languages that use the Latin alphabet represent the glottal stop with a reversed apostrophe, known as the ‘okina in Hawaiian. However, this reversed apostrophe is also used to transcribe the Arabic letter ‘ayin, which can lead to confusion. The reversed apostrophe is also the basis for the IPA character representing the voiced pharyngeal fricative. Features of the Glottal Stop: 1. Manner of Articulation: The glottal stop is classified as a plosive or stop consonant. This means it is produced by completely obstructing the airflow in the vocal tract and then releasing it. 2. Place of Articulation: The sound is glottal, meaning it is articulated at the level of the vocal folds. 3. Phonation Type: The glottal stop is voiceless, which indicates that it is produced without any vibration of the vocal cords. 4. Oral Consonant: It is an oral sound, meaning the airflow is allowed to escape exclusively through the mouth. 5. Central/Lateral Dichotomy: Since the glottal stop is articulated in the throat and does not involve any component in the oral cavity, the central versus lateral distinction does not apply. 6. Airstream Mechanism: The glottal stop is produced using a pulmonic egressive airstream mechanism. This means the sound is created by pushing air out of the lungs and through the vocal tract, rather than originating from the glottis or the mouth.
